modules.title: 1 · Panel data & unobserved heterogeneity
modules.summary: What panel data is, why repeated observations on the same entities help, and how an unobserved entity effect αᵢ creates correlation that biases naive regression.

stages.title: What makes data 'panel' data
stages.html:
Panel data: many entities, observed over time

A panel (or longitudinal) dataset follows the same units — people, firms, countries, schools — across multiple time periods. We index every observation by an entity i and a time t:

yᵢₜ = β₀ + β₁·xᵢₜ + αᵢ + εᵢₜ

Here yᵢₜ is the outcome for entity i at time t, and xᵢₜ is a regressor that can vary across both i and t. A balanced panel has every entity observed in every period: N entities × T periods = N·T rows.

The new ingredient: αᵢ

The term αᵢ is an entity effect — a quantity that is constant within an entity but differs across entities. Think of a firm's management quality, a person's innate ability, or a country's institutions. It is unobserved: we don't have a column for it, yet it shapes y.

  • εᵢₜ is ordinary idiosyncratic noise (varies over i and t).
  • αᵢ is fixed for the entity — it is the same in every period t for that i.
Key idea. Panel data's superpower: because we see each entity repeatedly, we can isolate and remove the time-invariant αᵢ even though we never measure it directly. Cross-sectional (one-shot) data cannot do this.

stages.title: Why αᵢ is dangerous: unobserved heterogeneity
stages.html:
Unobserved heterogeneity and omitted-variable bias

Regression gives unbiased slopes only when the regressor is uncorrelated with everything left in the error term. In the panel model, the composite error is αᵢ + εᵢₜ. The problem appears when the unobserved αᵢ is correlated with xᵢₜ:

Cov(xᵢₜ , αᵢ) ≠ 0

Then αᵢ is just an omitted variable that happens to be bundled with x. A regression of y on x alone will mistakenly credit x with variation that is really due to αᵢ.

A concrete story

Suppose y = wages, x = years of schooling, and αᵢ = unobserved ability. High-ability people both earn more (αᵢ pushes y up) and stay in school longer (αᵢ correlates with x). A naive wage-on-schooling regression blends the true return to schooling with the ability premium, overstating β₁.

  • If Cov(x, α) > 0, the naive slope is biased upward.
  • If Cov(x, α) < 0, it is biased downward.
  • If Cov(x, α) = 0, there is no bias from α (though it still inflates the variance of the error).
Key idea. The whole fixed-vs-random-effects debate is a debate about one quantity: is αᵢ correlated with xᵢₜ? If yes, you need fixed effects.

stages.title: Build a balanced panel and look at it
stages.note: We simulate N=40 entities over T=6 periods. The entity effect alpha is correlated with x (corr≈0.8), so x carries some of alpha's fingerprint. True slope = 2.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 40, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
time   = np.tile(np.arange(T), N)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)            # one entity effect per entity
# x is correlated with the entity's alpha:
x = 0.8*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)   # true beta1 = 2
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'time': time, 'x': x, 'y': y})
print('panel shape (rows, cols):', df.shape, ' = N*T =', N*T)
print(df.head(8).to_string(index=False))
print('\nCorr(x, alpha_i) =', round(np.corrcoef(x, alpha[entity])[0,1], 3))
# colour each entity's cloud so the vertical shifts (the alpha_i) are visible
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
for i in range(0, N, 8):
    m = df['entity']==i
    plt.scatter(df.x[m], df.y[m], s=18, label=f'entity {i}')
plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y'); plt.title('each entity = a shifted cloud (its own alpha_i)')
plt.legend(fontsize=7)

stages.title: Check: what is αᵢ?
stages.prompt: In yᵢₜ = β₀ + β₁·xᵢₜ + αᵢ + εᵢₜ, what distinguishes αᵢ from εᵢₜ?
choices: αᵢ varies over time within an entity; εᵢₜ is constant
αᵢ is constant within an entity but differs across entities; εᵢₜ varies over both i and t
αᵢ is observed in the data; εᵢₜ is unobserved
They are identical; the notation is redundant
stages.hint: The 'i' subscript with no 't' is the giveaway.
stages.explain: αᵢ carries only an i subscript, so it is fixed across all periods of entity i but differs from entity to entity. εᵢₜ carries both subscripts and is the usual time-varying noise. Both are unobserved.

stages.title: Check: when does αᵢ cause bias?
stages.prompt: A naive regression of y on x (ignoring αᵢ) gives a biased β₁ precisely when:
choices: αᵢ has large variance
T is small
Cov(xᵢₜ, αᵢ) ≠ 0
εᵢₜ is heteroskedastic
stages.hint: Bias comes from correlation between the regressor and the omitted term.
stages.explain: Bias arises from omitted-variable correlation: if x is correlated with the omitted αᵢ, the slope absorbs αᵢ's effect. A large but uncorrelated αᵢ only inflates variance, it does not bias the slope.

stages.title: Name the hidden entity effect
stages.prompt: The time-invariant, entity-specific term αᵢ that you cannot observe — a firm's culture, a person's innate ability — is called the unobserved ___ effect, and it is what biases naive regression when it moves with x.
stages.lead: You just saw each entity sit at its own height αᵢ, a fixed trait carried in every one of its observations.
stages.hint: It is the word for entities differing in fixed, unmeasured ways — not 'error', not 'noise'.
stages.explain: The αᵢ-is-just-noise trap. αᵢ is unobserved heterogeneity: a fixed entity trait, not random scatter. The tempting belief that it is ordinary error fails because error averages to zero and is uncorrelated with x, whereas αᵢ is a persistent level that can correlate with x — that correlation, not its mere presence, is what biases a naive regression. Boundary: if Cov(x, αᵢ)=0 the heterogeneity is harmless to consistency (RE territory); only correlated heterogeneity demands the within transform.

modules.title: 2 · Pooled OLS and its bias
modules.summary: Pooled OLS ignores the panel structure and treats αᵢ as part of the error. We show, in code and with a slider, that this biases β₁ whenever αᵢ correlates with x.

stages.title: Pooled OLS: pretend the panel is one big cross-section
stages.html:
Pooled OLS

The laziest estimator stacks all N·T rows and runs ordinary OLS as if every row were an independent draw:

yᵢₜ = β₀ + β₁·xᵢₜ + uᵢₜ , where uᵢₜ = αᵢ + εᵢₜ

This is just smf.ols("y ~ x", df). It throws the entity effect into the error term uᵢₜ and hopes for the best.

When is pooled OLS okay?

Pooled OLS is consistent only if the regressor is uncorrelated with the whole composite error, which requires Cov(xᵢₜ, αᵢ) = 0. If αᵢ is correlated with x, pooled OLS inherits exactly the omitted-variable bias from Module 1.

Key idea. Pooled OLS = OLS that buries αᵢ in the error. It is unbiased when αᵢ ⟂ x, and biased otherwise. There is also a second, milder problem even when it's unbiased — read on.

A second problem: clustered errors

Even if Cov(x, α)=0, every observation of entity i shares the same αᵢ. That makes the errors correlated within an entity (serial / cluster correlation), so the default OLS standard errors are wrong — usually too small. Practitioners cluster standard errors by entity. We focus on the slope bias here, but keep this in mind.

stages.title: Pooled OLS overshoots the true slope
stages.note: Same panel as Module 1 (true β₁ = 2, Corr(x, α) ≈ 0.8). Watch pooled OLS report a slope well above 2.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 40, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = 0.8*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)   # TRUE beta1 = 2
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
pooled = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit()
print('TRUE beta1        = 2.000')
print('Pooled OLS beta1  = %.3f' % pooled.params['x'], '  <-- biased upward')
print('Pooled intercept  = %.3f' % pooled.params['Intercept'])
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(df.x, df.y, s=10, color='#c9c6ac', alpha=.6)
xs = np.linspace(df.x.min(), df.x.max(), 50)
plt.plot(xs, pooled.params['Intercept']+pooled.params['x']*xs, color='#da9100', lw=2.5, label='pooled fit')
plt.plot(xs, 1 + 2.0*xs, color='#6f6b57', lw=2, ls='--', label='true line (slope 2)')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('pooled beta1 = %.2f  vs  true 2.00' % pooled.params['x'])

stages.title: Why the pooled line tilts too steeply
stages.html:
Seeing the bias geometrically

Recall each entity is a little cloud sitting at its own height αᵢ. Because x is correlated with αᵢ, entities with high x are also the entities with high αᵢ — their whole cloud sits higher up. The pooled regression line tries to pass through all clouds at once, so it tilts steeper than the true within-cloud relationship to reach those raised high-x clouds.

  • The between-entity variation (high-α clouds at high x) inflates the apparent slope.
  • The within-entity relationship — how y moves when x moves for a fixed entity — is the unbiased β₁ we actually want.
Key idea. Pooled OLS mixes the between-entity and within-entity signals. When αᵢ correlates with x, the between part is contaminated, so the mix is biased. Fixed effects (Module 3) will throw away the between part and keep only the clean within part.

stages.title: Slider: dial the αᵢ–x correlation
stages.note: Move the slider to change how strongly the entity effect loads onto x. The pooled slope is shown in the title; the true slope is always 2. At loading 0 pooled is fine; crank it up and pooled drifts away.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 30, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = {{corr}}*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
pooled = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit()
b = pooled.params['x']
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(df.x, df.y, s=10, color='#c9c6ac', alpha=.6)
xs = np.linspace(df.x.min(), df.x.max(), 50)
plt.plot(xs, pooled.params['Intercept']+b*xs, color='#da9100', lw=2.5, label='pooled')
plt.plot(xs, 1+2.0*xs, color='#6f6b57', lw=2, ls='--', label='true (2.0)')
plt.legend(); plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('pooled beta1 = %.2f   (true = 2.00)' % b)

stages.title: Check: direction of the bias
stages.prompt: You set the slider so α loads NEGATIVELY onto x (loading ≈ −1.5). What happens to the pooled slope relative to the true value of 2?
choices: It stays at 2 — the sign of the loading doesn't matter
It is biased upward (above 2)
It is biased downward (below 2)
It becomes exactly 0
stages.hint: Bias direction follows the sign of Cov(x, α).
stages.explain: A negative loading makes Cov(x, α) < 0, so high-x entities sit lower (low α). That flattens the apparent slope, pulling pooled OLS below the true value of 2.

stages.title: Pooled OLS: inefficient, or worse?
stages.prompt: When the entity effect αᵢ is correlated with the regressor, pooled OLS is not merely inefficient — its slope estimate β̂₁ is ___ and inconsistent.
stages.lead: You watched the pooled line tilt too steeply because high-x entities also sit at high αᵢ.
stages.hint: Inconsistency is the large-sample word; what is the finite-sample word for an estimate that is centered off-target?
stages.explain: The 'pooled OLS is just inefficient' trap. Correlated αᵢ is textbook omitted-variable bias, so β̂₁ is biased AND inconsistent — wrong in finite samples and still wrong as n→∞. The tempting belief that pooling only costs precision fails because the omitted αᵢ sits in the error and shares variation with x, tilting the slope. Boundary: if αᵢ were uncorrelated with x, pooled OLS would be merely inefficient (not biased) — efficiency loss only, which is exactly the RE case.

modules.title: 3 · Fixed effects: within transformation & entity dummies
modules.summary: Fixed effects estimate β₁ from within-entity variation only, sweeping out αᵢ. We do it two equivalent ways — entity dummies and hand-coded demeaning — and confirm both kill the bias.

stages.title: The within transformation: subtract each entity's mean
stages.html:
Fixed effects = use only within-entity variation

Start from the model and average it over time within each entity (the entity mean, denoted with a bar):

ȳᵢ = β₀ + β₁·x̄ᵢ + αᵢ + ε̄ᵢ

Now subtract this entity-mean equation from the original. The constant β₀ cancels, and crucially αᵢ − αᵢ = 0 — the troublesome entity effect vanishes:

(yᵢₜ − ȳᵢ) = β₁·(xᵢₜ − x̄ᵢ) + (εᵢₜ − ε̄ᵢ)

This is the within (fixed-effects) transformation. We regress demeaned y on demeaned x — with no intercept, since demeaning already removed it. Because αᵢ is gone, any correlation between αᵢ and x can no longer bias β₁.

Key idea. Demeaning within each entity removes everything that is constant within that entity — including the unobserved αᵢ. What remains is pure within-entity variation, which gives a consistent β₁ even when Cov(x, α) ≠ 0.

The cost

Anything that does not vary within an entity (gender, a country's geography, a time-invariant treatment) is also wiped out and cannot be estimated by FE. FE buys consistency for x by discarding between-entity information.

stages.title: Method A — entity dummies
stages.note: Add a dummy for each entity with C(entity). This literally fits a separate intercept per entity, so x's slope uses only within-entity movement. Compare to the biased pooled slope.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 40, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = 0.8*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)   # true beta1 = 2
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
pooled = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit()
fe_dum = smf.ols('y ~ x + C(entity)', df).fit()      # one intercept per entity
print('TRUE beta1            = 2.000')
print('Pooled OLS beta1      = %.3f  (biased)'    % pooled.params['x'])
print('FE (entity dummies)   = %.3f  (consistent)'% fe_dum.params['x'])
print('\nFE estimated %d entity intercepts (the alpha_i absorbed).' % N)
print('FE std error on x     = %.3f' % fe_dum.bse['x'])

stages.title: Method B — demean by hand, then OLS
stages.note: groupby('entity').transform('mean') gives each row its entity mean. Subtract it from y and x, then OLS WITHOUT a constant. The slope matches the dummy approach exactly.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.api as sm, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 40, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = 0.8*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
# within transformation: subtract each entity's own mean
df['y_dm'] = df['y'] - df.groupby('entity')['y'].transform('mean')
df['x_dm'] = df['x'] - df.groupby('entity')['x'].transform('mean')
within = sm.OLS(df['y_dm'], df['x_dm']).fit()   # NO constant: demeaning removed it
fe_dum = smf.ols('y ~ x + C(entity)', df).fit()
print('Within (hand demean) beta1 = %.4f' % within.params.iloc[0])
print('FE (entity dummies)  beta1 = %.4f' % fe_dum.params['x'])
print('--> identical slope: the two methods are algebraically the same.')
msg = '\nNote: the hand-demeaned SE = %.4f is slightly too SMALL because OLS' % within.bse.iloc[0]
print(msg)
print('did not subtract the N = %d degrees of freedom for the absorbed' % N)
print('entity intercepts. The dummy version SE = %.4f is the correct one.' % fe_dum.bse['x'])

stages.title: Slider: pooled drifts, fixed effects holds
stages.note: Same loading slider as Module 2, but now both estimators are shown. No matter how you move it, the FE slope stays pinned near the true value of 2 while pooled wanders.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.api as sm, statsmodels.formula.api as smf, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 30, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = {{corr}}*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
pooled = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit().params['x']
yd = df['y'] - df.groupby('entity')['y'].transform('mean')
xd = df['x'] - df.groupby('entity')['x'].transform('mean')
fe = sm.OLS(yd, xd).fit().params.iloc[0]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.axhline(2.0, color='#6f6b57', ls='--', lw=2, label='true = 2')
plt.bar(['pooled','fixed effects'], [pooled, fe], color=['#da9100','#af983f'])
plt.ylabel('estimated beta1'); plt.ylim(0, max(3.2, pooled+0.5))
plt.legend()
plt.title('pooled = %.2f   FE = %.2f   (true 2.00)' % (pooled, fe))

stages.title: Check: why no constant?
stages.prompt: After the within transformation (yᵢₜ − ȳᵢ) on (xᵢₜ − x̄ᵢ), why do we run OLS WITHOUT an intercept?
choices: An intercept would reintroduce αᵢ
Demeaning forces both variables to have mean zero, so the intercept is identically zero
statsmodels does not allow intercepts in panel models
To save a degree of freedom for the slope
stages.hint: What is the mean of a demeaned variable?
stages.explain: Subtracting each entity's mean makes the overall mean of both demeaned variables exactly zero, so any fitted intercept would be zero. We drop it (and the dummy method already fits per-entity intercepts that play that role).

stages.title: Check: what FE cannot estimate
stages.prompt: Your panel includes a regressor 'female' that never changes within a person. What does the fixed-effects (within) estimator do with its coefficient?
choices: Estimates it precisely
Cannot estimate it — demeaning wipes out any time-invariant regressor
Estimates it but with the wrong sign
Uses it as the entity effect
stages.hint: Demean a variable that is constant within an entity — what's left?
stages.explain: A within-entity-constant variable becomes all zeros after demeaning, so FE has no variation to estimate its coefficient. This is FE's main limitation; random effects (Module 4) can recover such coefficients if its assumption holds.

stages.title: Name the transformation
stages.prompt: The estimator that removes time-invariant unit confounders by subtracting each entity's own time-mean from every observation is the ___ (fixed-effects) estimator.
stages.lead: You just derived (yᵢₜ − ȳᵢ) = β₁·(xᵢₜ − x̄ᵢ) + (εᵢₜ − ε̄ᵢ): demeaning made αᵢ − αᵢ = 0 vanish.
stages.hint: It uses only the variation of x around each entity's own mean — its mirror image, the 'between' estimator, uses cross-entity means.
stages.explain: The within-vs-between mix-up. The within estimator demeans each entity, sweeping out everything constant per entity — including αᵢ — and so identifies β₁ from within-entity variation alone. The tempting confusion with the BETWEEN estimator fails because between uses only cross-entity means, the very channel αᵢ contaminates, so it cannot purge the heterogeneity. Boundary: within buys consistency but discards all between-entity (time-invariant) information, so any regressor constant within an entity is wiped out and unidentified.

stages.title: Can FE price a fixed trait?
stages.prompt: Because fixed effects is the consistent estimator under correlated αᵢ, it can also recover the coefficient on a time-invariant regressor such as a person's gender.
stages.hint: The within transform subtracts each entity's mean — what happens to a variable that never changes within an entity?
stages.explain: The 'FE estimates everything' trap. FE is consistent under correlated αᵢ, but the within demeaning that buys that consistency also subtracts off any variable constant within an entity — a time-invariant regressor becomes all zeros and drops out, so its coefficient is unidentified. The tempting belief fails on this exact margin: consistency for x is bought by discarding between-entity information, and a time-invariant trait lives entirely in that discarded between part. Boundary: to price a time-invariant regressor you need RE (or pooled OLS), which retains between-entity variation — at the cost of assuming Cov(x, αᵢ)=0.

stages.title: Smaller SEs, so use RE?
stages.prompt: You just confirmed fixed effects sweeps αᵢ away and stays consistent under correlated αᵢ. Even so, since random effects yields smaller standard errors, RE is the better estimator to report here.
stages.hint: RE's smaller standard errors are only meaningful if RE is centered on the truth — is it, when αᵢ correlates with x?
stages.explain: The efficiency-over-consistency trap, the central FE-vs-RE error. Under correlated αᵢ, RE is inconsistent, so its smaller standard errors describe a tight interval around the wrong value — consistency must come before efficiency. The seductive 'smaller SEs win' rule fails because precision is only a virtue once the estimator is centered on the truth, and demeaning is what guarantees that here. Boundary: RE's efficiency genuinely wins when Cov(x, αᵢ)=0 (Hausman fails to reject), where both estimators are consistent and RE is simply tighter.

modules.title: 4 · Random effects & choosing FE vs RE
modules.summary: Random effects treats αᵢ as random noise uncorrelated with x, gaining efficiency and time-invariant coefficients — but only if that assumption holds. The Hausman idea tells you which to trust.

stages.title: Random effects: αᵢ as a random draw
stages.html:
The random-effects model

Random effects (RE) keeps the same equation but makes a strong assumption about αᵢ:

yᵢₜ = β₀ + β₁·xᵢₜ + αᵢ + εᵢₜ , with Cov(xᵢₜ, αᵢ) = 0

RE treats αᵢ as a random entity-specific intercept drawn from a distribution with variance σ²_α, uncorrelated with x. Estimation is by (feasible) GLS, which is equivalent to a partial demeaning: subtract a fraction θ of each entity mean, where

θ = 1 − √( σ²_ε / (σ²_ε + T·σ²_α) )

FE vs RE as two extremes of partial demeaning

  • Pooled OLS subtracts θ = 0 of the entity mean (no demeaning).
  • Fixed effects subtracts θ = 1 (full demeaning).
  • Random effects picks θ between 0 and 1 — a data-driven compromise.
Key idea. If Cov(x, α) = 0, RE is the best estimator: it is consistent like FE but more efficient (smaller standard errors), and it can estimate time-invariant regressors. If Cov(x, α) ≠ 0, RE is biased — only FE survives.

stages.title: Random effects via MixedLM (αᵢ ⟂ x)
stages.note: When the entity effect is genuinely uncorrelated with x, RE and FE agree on the slope, but RE reports a smaller standard error. We fit a random-intercept model with mixedlm and compare to the correctly-counted FE standard error (the dummy version).
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 50, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)                 # loading = 0: alpha independent of x
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
# Fixed effects via entity dummies (gives the CORRECT standard error)
fe = smf.ols('y ~ x + C(entity)', df).fit()
# Random effects: random intercept per entity
re = smf.mixedlm('y ~ x', df, groups=df['entity']).fit()
print('TRUE beta1 = 2.000   (here Cov(x, alpha) = 0)')
print('FE  beta1 = %.3f   SE = %.3f' % (fe.params['x'], fe.bse['x']))
print('RE  beta1 = %.3f   SE = %.3f' % (re.params['x'], re.bse['x']))
print('\nEstimated entity-effect variance (Group Var) = %.3f' % re.cov_re.iloc[0,0])
print('--> slopes agree; RE has the smaller SE, so it is more efficient here.')

stages.title: Now break RE's assumption: αᵢ correlates with x
stages.note: Reintroduce correlation between alpha and x. RE (like pooled) is now biased; only FE recovers 2. This divergence is exactly what a Hausman test detects.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.api as sm, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 50, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = 0.9*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)   # loading != 0: RE assumption FAILS
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
yd = df['y'] - df.groupby('entity')['y'].transform('mean')
xd = df['x'] - df.groupby('entity')['x'].transform('mean')
fe = sm.OLS(yd, xd).fit().params.iloc[0]
re = smf.mixedlm('y ~ x', df, groups=df['entity']).fit().params['x']
print('TRUE beta1 = 2.000   (Cov(x, alpha) != 0)')
print('FE  beta1 = %.3f   <- still consistent' % fe)
print('RE  beta1 = %.3f   <- biased away from 2' % re)
print('\nThe gap |FE - RE| = %.3f signals RE is inconsistent here.' % abs(fe-re))
print('A large gap => prefer FE (this is the Hausman intuition).')

stages.title: The Hausman idea: let the gap decide
stages.html:
Choosing FE vs RE: the Hausman intuition

The two estimators react differently to a correlated αᵢ:

  • FE is consistent whether or not Cov(x, α) = 0 — it always demeans αᵢ away. Its price is lost efficiency and no time-invariant coefficients.
  • RE is consistent and efficient only if Cov(x, α) = 0. If that fails, RE is biased.

So compare them. Under the RE assumption both estimate the same β₁, so β̂_FE − β̂_RE should be small (just sampling noise). If the assumption fails, RE is pulled away while FE stays put, and the gap grows.

H = (β̂_FE − β̂_RE)′ · [Var(β̂_FE) − Var(β̂_RE)]⁻¹ · (β̂_FE − β̂_RE)

This Hausman statistic is large when the estimators disagree. A large H (small p-value) rejects RE → use fixed effects. A small H means RE and FE agree, so you may keep the more efficient random effects.

Decision rule. Estimators disagree (large Hausman) → trust FE. Estimators agree (small Hausman) → RE is safe and more efficient. When in doubt, or when α plausibly correlates with x (the usual case in economics), default to FE.

Practical checklist

  • Need a coefficient on a time-invariant variable? RE (or pooled) is your only option — FE cannot give it.
  • Worried about unobserved confounders correlated with x? FE is the safe, robust choice.
  • Either way, cluster standard errors by entity to handle within-entity correlation.

stages.title: Slider: watch FE and RE diverge
stages.note: As the α–x loading grows, RE (and pooled) drift from the true 2, while FE stays put. The growing FE–RE gap is the engine of the Hausman test.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, statsmodels.api as sm, statsmodels.formula.api as smf, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, T = 40, 6
entity = np.repeat(np.arange(N), T)
alpha  = rng.normal(0, 2, N)
x = {{corr}}*alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
y = 1 + 2.0*x + alpha[entity] + rng.normal(0, 1, N*T)
df = pd.DataFrame({'entity': entity, 'x': x, 'y': y})
pooled = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit().params['x']
yd = df['y'] - df.groupby('entity')['y'].transform('mean')
xd = df['x'] - df.groupby('entity')['x'].transform('mean')
fe = sm.OLS(yd, xd).fit().params.iloc[0]
re = smf.mixedlm('y ~ x', df, groups=df['entity']).fit().params['x']
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.axhline(2.0, color='#6f6b57', ls='--', lw=2, label='true = 2')
plt.bar(['pooled','RE','FE'], [pooled, re, fe], color=['#c9c6ac','#da9100','#af983f'])
plt.ylabel('estimated beta1'); plt.ylim(0, max(3.4, pooled+0.5)); plt.legend()
plt.title('FE=%.2f  RE=%.2f  gap=%.2f' % (fe, re, abs(fe-re)))

stages.title: Check: reading the Hausman result
stages.prompt: A Hausman test returns a large statistic (p-value ≈ 0.001), meaning FE and RE estimates differ sharply. What should you conclude?
choices: RE is fine and more efficient — keep RE
Reject RE; αᵢ is correlated with x, so use fixed effects
Both estimators are biased; use pooled OLS
Increase T and re-run RE
stages.hint: A big gap means RE's zero-correlation assumption is failing.
stages.explain: A large Hausman statistic signals the estimators disagree, which happens when Cov(x, α) ≠ 0 and RE is inconsistent. You reject RE and rely on the always-consistent fixed-effects estimator.

stages.title: Check: when RE wins
stages.prompt: You need the effect of a time-invariant regressor (e.g. a person's birth region) AND a Hausman test does not reject RE. Which estimator do you use?
choices: Fixed effects — it is always safest
Random effects — it is consistent here and, unlike FE, can estimate time-invariant regressors
Pooled OLS — it ignores αᵢ
Neither is identified
stages.hint: FE demeans away time-invariant variables; RE does not.
stages.explain: When Hausman does not reject (αᵢ ⟂ x), RE is consistent and efficient, and crucially it retains time-invariant regressors that FE would wipe out — so RE is the right choice.

stages.title: Hausman rejects RE — now what?
stages.prompt: Your panel has plausibly Cov(x, αᵢ) ≠ 0, and the Hausman test returns a large statistic (p = 0.002), so β̂_FE and β̂_RE disagree sharply. Which estimator should you report for β₁?
choices: Random effects, because it is more efficient (smaller standard errors)
Random effects, because the Hausman test confirms its assumption holds
Fixed effects, because it stays consistent whether or not αᵢ correlates with x
Pooled OLS, because it uses all the variation in the data
why: The efficiency-over-consistency trap: smaller SEs around a biased center are worthless.
Backwards — a large Hausman statistic REJECTS RE's assumption, it does not confirm it.
Pooled OLS is the most biased here; using more variation includes the contaminated between-entity part.
stages.hint: A large Hausman statistic means the two estimators disagree — which one is the one that survives correlated αᵢ?
stages.explain: The efficiency-over-consistency trap, the central FE-vs-RE error. A large Hausman statistic rejects RE's Cov(x, αᵢ)=0 assumption, so RE is inconsistent here and you report fixed effects, which demeans αᵢ away regardless of correlation. The seductive belief 'RE has smaller standard errors, so prefer it' fails because efficiency is worthless around a biased center — a tight interval on the wrong number. Boundary: RE's efficiency is real and decisive ONLY when Hausman fails to reject (small statistic), i.e. when αᵢ truly is uncorrelated with x.

stages.title: RE by default?
stages.prompt: Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects, so you should prefer random effects by default.
stages.hint: Efficiency is a property RE only has WHEN one assumption holds — what is that assumption, and is it usually safe in economics?
stages.explain: The efficiency-over-consistency trap. RE is more efficient, but only IF Cov(x, αᵢ)=0; when αᵢ correlates with x — the usual reason you reached for panel data — RE is inconsistent, and consistency must come before efficiency. The tempting 'smaller SEs win' rule fails because a precise estimate centered on the wrong value is worse than an imprecise unbiased one; the Hausman test adjudicates exactly this. Boundary: 'default to RE' is sound only after Hausman fails to reject, or when you specifically need a time-invariant coefficient FE cannot deliver.
